stem: The Revolt of 1857 began among the sepoys at which cantonment on 10 May 1857?
solution: The mutiny broke out at Meerut on 10 May 1857, from where the sepoys marched to Delhi.

stem: The immediate spark for the revolt was the introduction of the new Enfield rifle, whose cartridges were believed to be greased with:
options: The fat of cows and pigs
solution: Sepoys believed the cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat — offensive to both Hindus and Muslims — as they had to bite them open.

stem: The sepoy who attacked his officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 and became an early martyr of the revolt was:
solution: Mangal Pandey of the 34th Native Infantry rebelled at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 and was hanged on 8 April 1857.

stem: Mangal Pandey was executed (hanged) on:
solution: Mangal Pandey was hanged on 8 April 1857, shortly after his act of defiance at Barrackpore.

stem: After capturing Delhi, the rebels proclaimed which person as their leader/emperor?
solution: The rebel sepoys proclaimed the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, as their symbolic leader.

stem: The rebellion at Kanpur was led by:
solution: Nana Saheb, the adopted son of the late Peshwa Baji Rao II, led the revolt at Kanpur.

stem: Nana Saheb was the adopted son of which former ruler?
solution: Nana Saheb was the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II; the British had refused him his father's pension, fuelling his rebellion.

stem: The revolt at Jhansi was led by:
solution: Rani Lakshmibai led the revolt at Jhansi, fighting valiantly against the British.

stem: The leader of the revolt at Lucknow (Awadh) was:
solution: Begum Hazrat Mahal led the uprising in Lucknow, proclaiming her son Birjis Qadr as ruler of Awadh.

stem: Kunwar Singh, an aged leader of the revolt, belonged to which region?
solution: Kunwar Singh, a zamindar of Jagdishpur (Arrah) in Bihar, was a prominent leader of the 1857 revolt despite his old age.

stem: The able military commander who led the rebel forces in Delhi was:
solution: General Bakht Khan took charge of the rebel military organisation in Delhi under the nominal leadership of Bahadur Shah Zafar.

stem: The close associate of Nana Saheb who continued guerrilla resistance and was executed in 1859 was:
solution: Tantia Tope, an aide of Nana Saheb, carried on the fight after major defeats and was captured and executed in 1859.

stem: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi died fighting in:
solution: Rani Lakshmibai died in battle near Gwalior in June 1858.

stem: The leader of the revolt in the Faizabad region, a religious figure, was:
solution: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah was an important leader of the revolt in the Awadh/Faizabad region.

stem: One major political cause of the revolt was the British policy of annexing states, especially the:
options: Doctrine of Lapse and the annexation of Awadh (1856)
solution: Annexations under the Doctrine of Lapse and the takeover of Awadh in 1856 caused deep resentment among rulers and people alike.

stem: Awadh, whose annexation in 1856 angered many, had been taken over on the grounds of:
solution: Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the pretext of 'misgovernment', deeply offending its ruler Wajid Ali Shah and the people of Awadh.

stem: A social/religious cause of the revolt was the fear among Indians that the British intended to:
options: Convert them to Christianity and interfere with their religion and customs
solution: Missionary activity and social reforms bred a fear that the British aimed to destroy Indian religions and convert people to Christianity.

stem: The British recaptured Delhi from the rebels in:
solution: British forces retook Delhi in September 1857 after fierce fighting.

stem: After the fall of Delhi, Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried and exiled to:
solution: Bahadur Shah Zafar was captured, tried, and exiled to Rangoon (present-day Yangon, Myanmar), where he died in 1862.

stem: Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, died in exile in:
solution: Bahadur Shah Zafar died in Rangoon in 1862, marking the formal end of the Mughal dynasty.

stem: As a direct result of the revolt, the British Crown took over the governance of India from the East India Company through the:
solution: The Government of India Act 1858 ended Company rule and transferred power over India to the British Crown.

stem: Under the post-1858 arrangement, the Governor-General of India was also given the new title of:
solution: The Governor-General now also served as the Viceroy, representing the British Crown in India.

stem: The first Viceroy of India was:
solution: Lord Canning, who was Governor-General during the revolt, became the first Viceroy of India after 1858.

stem: A new office created in Britain in 1858 to manage Indian affairs was that of the:
solution: The post of Secretary of State for India, assisted by the India Council, was created in Britain to oversee the administration of India.

stem: After 1858, the British abandoned which policy of annexation to reassure Indian princes?
solution: The Doctrine of Lapse was given up; princes were assured their territory would not be annexed and were allowed to pass their kingdoms to heirs, including adopted sons.

stem: The 1858 Proclamation of Queen Victoria promised, among other things, to:
options: Respect the rights of Indian princes and not interfere in religious matters
solution: Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) pledged to honour the treaties with princes and to respect Indians' religions and customs.

stem: After the revolt, the British reorganised the army by:
options: Reducing the number of European soldiers
Increasing the proportion of European soldiers and recruiting more selectively
solution: The army was restructured with a higher proportion of European troops and recruitment shifted away from regions seen as rebellious, following a 'divide and rule' approach.

stem: The revolt was largely concentrated in which part of India?
options: North and Central India (the Ganga valley and nearby regions)
solution: The uprising was strongest in north and central India (Delhi, Awadh, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bihar), while much of the south, Punjab and Bengal remained largely quiet.

stem: V. D. Savarkar, in his 1909 book, described the events of 1857 as the:
solution: V. D. Savarkar called 1857 the 'First War of Indian Independence' in his 1909 book, challenging the British label 'Sepoy Mutiny'.

stem: One economic grievance behind the revolt was that British policies had ruined many:
options: Artisans and weavers, and burdened peasants with heavy taxes
solution: British manufactured goods ruined Indian artisans/weavers, while heavy land revenue impoverished peasants — feeding widespread discontent.

stem: Indian sepoys had specific grievances such as:
options: Low pay, poor prospects, and being asked to serve overseas against their beliefs
solution: Sepoys resented low pay, limited promotion, racial discrimination, and rules (like overseas service) that clashed with their religious beliefs.

stem: The talukdars and landholders of Awadh joined the revolt largely because:
options: They had lost their estates and power after the British annexation and land settlement
They had no interest in land
solution: After Awadh's annexation, the British dispossessed many talukdars of their estates, so they rallied to the revolt to regain their lost power.

stem: Which Indian ruler is an example of those who helped the British suppress the revolt?
solution: Several rulers, such as the Scindia of Gwalior and the Nizam of Hyderabad, sided with the British and helped suppress the revolt.

stem: The British suppression of the revolt was marked by:
options: Severe reprisals, executions and destruction in rebel areas
solution: The British crushed the revolt with great severity, carrying out harsh reprisals, executions and destruction across the rebel regions.

stem: The son of Begum Hazrat Mahal, proclaimed as the ruler of Awadh during the revolt, was:
solution: Begum Hazrat Mahal proclaimed her young son Birjis Qadr as the ruler of Awadh during the uprising.

stem: The British policy after 1857 of favouring some groups and mistrusting others (especially Muslims, blamed for the revolt) is an example of:
solution: The post-revolt strategy of playing communities and regions against one another is described as a 'divide and rule' policy.

stem: Why did the greased cartridge issue provoke such strong reaction among sepoys?
options: It offended the religious feelings of both Hindu and Muslim soldiers
solution: Biting cartridges greased with cow fat (offending Hindus) and pig fat (offending Muslims) was seen as an attack on the religion of the sepoys.

stem: The revolt of 1857 is significant in Indian history because it:
options: Was the first large-scale, though unsuccessful, challenge to British rule and shaped later nationalism
solution: Though suppressed, 1857 was the first major, widespread challenge to colonial rule and became a source of inspiration for later nationalist movements.

stem: After the revolt, the British increasingly relied on the support of which groups to secure their rule?
options: Loyal princes, big landholders and zamindars
solution: The British cultivated the loyalty of princes and landholders, restoring some privileges to bind them to the colonial order.

stem: Which of the following pairs of leader and centre of revolt is correctly matched?
solution: Rani Lakshmibai led at Jhansi. Nana Saheb was at Kanpur, Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow, and Kunwar Singh in Bihar.

stem: The revolt failed partly because:
options: It lacked unified leadership, common planning and support from all regions and groups
solution: The rebels lacked central coordination, a common goal and nationwide support; many regions and rulers stayed loyal to the British, contributing to its failure.

stem: The last Mughal emperor's role in the revolt shows that rebels sought legitimacy by:
options: Rallying around an old, recognised symbol of authority (the Mughal emperor)
solution: By proclaiming Bahadur Shah Zafar as emperor, the rebels sought to unite under a traditional, widely-recognised symbol of Indian sovereignty.

stem: The Government of India Act 1858 transferred the power of the Company to the Crown and ended the rule of the:
solution: The Act of 1858 abolished the rule of the East India Company and placed India directly under the British Crown.

stem: Which statement about the geographic spread of the revolt is correct?
options: Punjab, Bengal and most of the south remained largely unaffected
The whole of India rose together
solution: The revolt was concentrated in the north-central belt; Punjab, Bengal and most of southern India remained largely calm.

stem: The British removed which symbolic institution as a consequence of the revolt?
solution: With Bahadur Shah Zafar's exile and death, the Mughal dynasty was formally ended by the British after the revolt.

stem: The pension dispute that turned Nana Saheb against the British arose because they:
options: Refused to continue the pension of his adoptive father, the Peshwa
solution: The British refused to pay Nana Saheb the pension that had been granted to his adoptive father, the last Peshwa, angering him.

stem: After 1858, the British promised to respect the religions and customs of Indians mainly to:
options: Prevent another revolt by reassuring the population
solution: To avoid provoking another uprising, the Crown promised religious non-interference and respect for Indian customs.

stem: Which of the following best describes the change in the nature of the revolt after it began?
options: It stayed confined to the army
It spread from the sepoys to involve peasants, artisans, zamindars and ordinary people in many areas
It became a purely religious festival
It turned into a trade dispute
solution: Beginning as a military mutiny, the revolt broadened into a popular uprising drawing in peasants, artisans, talukdars and common people in the affected regions.

stem: The British labelled the events of 1857 the 'Sepoy Mutiny' because they wished to portray it as:
options: A mere revolt of soldiers rather than a widespread popular rebellion
solution: Calling it a 'mutiny' downplayed it as an army revolt, denying its character as a broad-based challenge to colonial rule.

stem: The new Enfield rifle cartridges were rumoured to be greased with:
options: The fat of cows and pigs
solution: The ENFIELD cartridges were rumoured to be greased with the FAT of COWS and PIGS, offending both Hindu and Muslim sepoys who had to bite them open. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Mangal Pandey, who sparked the initial mutiny, was stationed at:
solution: MANGAL PANDEY was stationed at BARRACKPORE, where he attacked his officers on 29 March 1857. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Revolt of 1857 formally began with the mutiny of sepoys at Meerut on:
solution: The Revolt began at MEERUT on 10 MAY 1857, from where sepoys marched to Delhi. So option 1 is correct.

stem: After capturing Delhi, the rebels proclaimed as their symbolic leader the Mughal emperor:
solution: The rebels proclaimed BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR, the last Mughal emperor, as their symbolic leader. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Match List-I (Leader) with List-II (Centre of revolt): P. Nana Saheb Q. Rani Lakshmibai R. Begum Hazrat Mahal S. Kunwar Singh | 1. Jhansi 2. Kanpur 3. Bihar (Arrah) 4. Lucknow (Awadh)
solution: Nana Saheb → Kanpur (P-2); Rani Lakshmibai → Jhansi (Q-1); Begum Hazrat Mahal → Lucknow/Awadh (R-4); Kunwar Singh → Bihar/Arrah (S-3). So option 1 is correct.

stem: Nana Saheb was the adopted son of the former Peshwa:
solution: NANA SAHEB was the adopted son of the last Peshwa, BAJI RAO II, and rebelled after being denied his pension. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The able rebel military commander who led forces in Delhi was:
solution: General BAKHT KHAN led the rebel forces in DELHI. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The close associate of Nana Saheb who carried on guerrilla resistance and was captured and executed in 1859 was:
solution: TANTIA TOPE, Nana Saheb's associate, carried on GUERRILLA resistance and was captured and EXECUTED in 1859. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi died fighting the British in:
solution: RANI LAKSHMIBAI died fighting in 1858, near GWALIOR. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The religious leader who led the revolt in the Faizabad/Awadh region was:
solution: MAULVI AHMADULLAH SHAH led the revolt in the FAIZABAD/Awadh region. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Kunwar Singh, an aged leader of the revolt, belonged to:
solution: KUNWAR SINGH belonged to BIHAR (Jagdishpur/Arrah). So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The Doctrine of Lapse was a political cause of the 1857 revolt. Reason (R): The annexation of states like Jhansi, Satara and Nagpur angered many Indian rulers. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: A is TRUE — the Doctrine of Lapse was a cause. R is TRUE and EXPLAINS A: the ANNEXATION of JHANSI, SATARA, and NAGPUR angered many rulers. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Consider the following causes of the 1857 revolt: 1. Political (annexations) 2. Economic (ruin of artisans, high taxes) 3. Religious/social (fear of conversion) 4. Military (sepoy grievances). How many are valid causes?
solution: ALL FOUR — POLITICAL, ECONOMIC, RELIGIOUS/SOCIAL, and MILITARY — were valid causes of the 1857 revolt. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The recapture of Delhi in September 1857 was significant because Delhi was:
options: The symbolic heart of the revolt under the Mughal emperor
solution: DELHI was the SYMBOLIC HEART of the revolt under BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR, so its recapture was a major British victory. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The sons and grandson of Bahadur Shah Zafar were:
options: Shot dead by the British officer Hodson
solution: The SONS and GRANDSON of Bahadur Shah Zafar were SHOT DEAD by the British officer HODSON after the fall of Delhi. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Government of India Act 1858 transferred power over India from the Company to the:
solution: The GOVERNMENT of INDIA ACT 1858 transferred power from the COMPANY to the BRITISH CROWN. So option 1 is correct.

stem: After 1858, the top British representative in India was titled:
solution: After 1858, the Governor-General was also given the title of VICEROY, representing the Crown. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A new British cabinet post created in 1858 to oversee Indian affairs was the:
solution: The SECRETARY of STATE for INDIA was created in 1858 to manage Indian affairs, assisted by a council. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 1858 Proclamation of Queen Victoria promised to:
options: Respect Indians' religions and customs and end further annexations
solution: Queen Victoria's 1858 PROCLAMATION promised to RESPECT Indians' RELIGIONS and CUSTOMS and END further ANNEXATIONS. So option 1 is correct.

stem: After 1858, the British abandoned which annexation policy to reassure Indian rulers?
solution: After 1858, the British ABANDONED the DOCTRINE of LAPSE to reassure Indian princes. So option 1 is correct.

stem: After 1857, the British recruited more soldiers from groups they now considered loyal, such as the:
solution: After 1857 the British favoured recruiting SIKHS and GURKHAS, considered loyal, while reducing reliance on the Bengal army. So option 1 is correct.

stem: V.D. Savarkar, in his 1909 book, described 1857 as:
options: The First War of Indian Independence
solution: V.D. SAVARKAR called 1857 'The FIRST WAR of INDIAN INDEPENDENCE'. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The British called the events of 1857 a 'Sepoy Mutiny' because they wished to:
options: Portray it as a limited army revolt, not a popular national uprising
solution: The British called it a 'SEPOY MUTINY' to portray it as a LIMITED ARMY REVOLT, not a POPULAR NATIONAL UPRISING. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Begum Hazrat Mahal led the revolt at Lucknow in the name of her young son:
solution: BEGUM HAZRAT MAHAL led the revolt in Lucknow in the name of her son BIRJIS QADR, proclaimed ruler of Awadh. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of alleged:
solution: AWADH was annexed in 1856 on the ground of alleged MISGOVERNANCE by the Nawab, deeply angering its people. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The talukdars (landholders) of Awadh joined the revolt largely because:
options: Their estates and power had been taken away after annexation
solution: The TALUKDARS of Awadh joined because their ESTATES and POWER had been TAKEN AWAY after annexation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): Many artisans and weavers were sympathetic to the revolt. Reason (R): British economic policies and cheap machine-made goods had ruined their livelihoods. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: A is TRUE — artisans sympathised with the revolt. R is TRUE and EXPLAINS A: British ECONOMIC POLICIES and CHEAP MACHINE-MADE goods had RUINED their livelihoods. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following rulers HELPED the British suppress the revolt?
options: Scindia of Gwalior and the Nizam of Hyderabad
solution: The SCINDIA of GWALIOR and the NIZAM of HYDERABAD (among others) HELPED the British SUPPRESS the revolt. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The revolt of 1857 was largely concentrated in:
options: North and central India (Delhi, Awadh, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bihar)
solution: The revolt was largely concentrated in NORTH and CENTRAL INDIA — Delhi, Awadh, Kanpur, Jhansi, and Bihar. So option 1 is correct.

stem: One reason the rebels were militarily disadvantaged was that they:
options: Lacked modern weapons, coordination and a common plan against the disciplined British army
Had more cannons than the British
solution: The rebels LACKED MODERN WEAPONS, COORDINATION, and a COMMON PLAN against the DISCIPLINED British army, a key military disadvantage. So option 1 is correct.

stem: After 1857, the British increasingly relied on the support of:
solution: After 1857, the British relied on PRINCES, LANDLORDS, and 'LOYAL' groups to maintain control. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Consider the pairs: 1. Mangal Pandey — Barrackpore 2. Bahadur Shah Zafar — Delhi 3. Rani Lakshmibai — Jhansi. How many are correctly matched?
solution: ALL THREE match: MANGAL PANDEY → Barrackpore; BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR → Delhi; RANI LAKSHMIBAI → Jhansi. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The greased-cartridge issue provoked strong reaction because sepoys had to:
options: Bite off the cartridge, believing it was greased with cow and pig fat, violating their religion
solution: Sepoys had to BITE OFF the cartridge, believed to be greased with COW and PIG FAT, VIOLATING Hindu and Muslim religious feelings. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The revolt of 1857 is historically significant because it:
options: Was the first large-scale, united challenge to British rule and led to major changes in governance
solution: 1857 was the FIRST large-scale, UNITED CHALLENGE to British rule and led to MAJOR CHANGES in governance (Crown rule). So option 1 is correct.

stem: To crush the revolt, the British passed laws that allowed them to:
options: Try and punish rebels swiftly and impose martial law
solution: The British passed harsh LAWS allowing SWIFT TRIALS, PUNISHMENT of rebels, and MARTIAL LAW to crush the revolt. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The last Mughal emperor's role as figurehead shows that the rebels sought:
options: Legitimacy by rallying around a traditional symbol of authority
solution: By rallying around BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR, the rebels sought LEGITIMACY through a TRADITIONAL SYMBOL of AUTHORITY. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Bahadur Shah Zafar died in exile in:
solution: BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR died in exile (Rangoon) in 1862. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Nana Saheb's grievance against the British is an example of how the revolt drew in leaders who had lost:
options: Titles, pensions and privileges under colonial policy
solution: NANA SAHEB's case shows the revolt drew in leaders who had LOST TITLES, PENSIONS, and PRIVILEGES under colonial policy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: After the revolt, the ratio of British to Indian soldiers in the army was:
options: Increased in favour of British soldiers
solution: After the revolt, the RATIO of BRITISH to Indian soldiers was INCREASED in favour of BRITISH troops, to prevent another mutiny. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which statement about the nature of the 1857 revolt is most accurate?
options: It began as a sepoy mutiny but grew into a widespread civil and popular rebellion in many areas
It was purely a peasant movement
solution: 1857 BEGAN as a SEPOY MUTINY but GREW into a WIDESPREAD CIVIL and POPULAR rebellion in many areas. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The 1857 revolt failed to end British rule. Reason (R): However, it forced the British to change how they governed India. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: A is TRUE — the revolt failed to end British rule. R is TRUE — it forced governance changes. But R does not EXPLAIN why A (the failure) happened; they are two separate facts. So option 2 is correct.

stem: With the exile of Bahadur Shah Zafar in 1858, the ______ dynasty came to a formal end.
solution: With the exile of BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR (1858), the MUGHAL dynasty came to a formal END. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The transfer of power to the Crown in 1858 meant Indian administration was now run:
options: Directly by the British government through the Viceroy and Secretary of State
solution: After 1858, Indian administration was run DIRECTLY by the BRITISH GOVERNMENT through the VICEROY and SECRETARY of STATE. So option 1 is correct.

stem: One social/religious cause of the revolt was the fear that the British intended to:
options: Convert Indians to Christianity and interfere with their customs
solution: A social/religious cause was the FEAR that the British wanted to CONVERT Indians to CHRISTIANITY and INTERFERE with their customs. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The British policy after 1857 of favouring some communities while mistrusting others contributed to:
solution: The post-1857 policy of FAVOURING some and MISTRUSTING others contributed to a 'DIVIDE and RULE' approach. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which leader-and-centre pairing is correctly matched?
solution: Only 'BAKHT KHAN — DELHI' is correct. Lakshmibai = Jhansi; Hazrat Mahal = Lucknow; Kunwar Singh = Bihar. So option 1 is correct.

stem: One economic grievance behind the revolt was that British policies had ruined the:
solution: An economic grievance was that British policies had RUINED the TRADITIONAL HANDICRAFT and WEAVING industries. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The events of 1857 are also referred to by nationalists as the:
options: First War of Independence / Great Revolt
solution: Nationalists refer to 1857 as the FIRST WAR of INDEPENDENCE or the GREAT REVOLT. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall consequence of 1857 for the structure of British rule was that India came under:
options: Direct, more centralised control of the British Crown and Parliament
solution: After 1857, India was governed directly by the British Crown through the Viceroy and the Secretary of State — a more centralised imperial administration.
